items.title: 8.15 Effect of a catalyst on equilibrium

source_refs.note: Topic 8.15, printed page 182 (Figure 8.3, carried by the Le Chatelier original).

blocks.title: Catalyst
blocks.text: A catalyst is a substance which increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself being consumed. It does not change the equilibrium position or the equilibrium constant of a reaction; it speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is attained, so the yield of the reaction stays the same.

A catalyst provides a new path of lower activation energy. On a graph of potential energy against reaction coordinate the maximum of the curve is lower in the presence of a catalyst: the activation energy of the uncatalysed reaction, Ea, is replaced by a smaller Ea' for the catalysed one, for both the forward and the reverse reaction, while the energies of reactants and products, and so delta H, are unchanged.

blocks.prompt: Adding V2O5 to the SO2 and O2 mixture of the contact process makes SO3 form much faster. Does it increase the equilibrium yield of SO3?
blocks.explanation: No. The catalyst lowers the activation energy of both the forward and the reverse reaction equally, so equilibrium is reached sooner but at the same position; the yield at equilibrium and Kp are unchanged. The yield can be raised only by changing temperature, pressure or concentrations.

items: A catalyst speeds the approach to equilibrium by lowering Ea for both directions, but leaves the position, the constant and the yield unchanged (Figure 8.3).
